newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico's Alestra says to avoid price war.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico's Alestra says to avoid price war.

text.p: Mexico's Alestra, a new entrant on the recently opened telephone market, said it plans to boost market share without resorting to a price war.

"We do not plan to add fuel to the fire. Our goal is to have the market recognize the value of Alestra's services, of AT&T's services," said Alejandro Rodriguez, marketing vice-president at Alestra, made up of AT&T, Mexican industrial firm Alfa and holding group VISA-Bancomer.
Mexico's telephone market began opening up on January 1. It will be completely open to competition by mid-year.
For decades, customers could only use former monopoly Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex).
Alestra recently undercut its rivals' prices, including Telmex, by setting domestic long-distance rates of 95 centavos per minute during non-peak hours and 1.90 pesos per minute during peak hours.
A few weeks later, MCI Communications -backed Avantel adjusted its price downward to that of Alestra.
"Obviously, we can't be out of a sensible market range of pricing, but we weren't looking to be the cheapest," Rodriguez said.
Alestra has invested $450 million in laying down some 4,300 km of fiber-optic cable in 24 different cities, Rodriguez said.
Some industry analysts have said Alestra did not have as aggressive a start as Avantel due to funding problems and the addition of new partners into the company.
Rodriguez said the company was in-line with its schedule and would be ready to provide service to each city as the market opens up. It plans to invest at total of $1 billion by the end of 1998.
"We are going to invest whatever is needed because this company's partners are dedicated to doing this right," he said.
Rodriguez declined to say how much market share Alestra hoped to capture from Telmex.

The first city to open to competition was Queretaro, where residents have been balloted over their preferred long-distance carriers. The process has led to rival claims over market shares based on preliminary estimates of ballot returns.
According to an independent firm in charge of presubsrciption, 42 percent of returns in Queretaro as of Dec 30, 1996, favored Alestra, Rodriguez said.
"The ballots do not imply market share, but are nonetheless an indication of efforts made... It is a number that is there, we did not invent it," he said.
